body.heading: Why side by side works
paragraphs: Walking together puts two people shoulder to shoulder, looking at the same world instead of at each other. For many of us that lowers the stakes of talking: thoughts arrive at walking pace, silences are comfortable, and difficult sentences are easier to say to the horizon than to a face.
There is no table to clear and no clock on it. The conversation can end at the front door, which makes starting it feel safer.

body.heading: Short routes, regular times
paragraphs: A loop of twenty minutes is enough. Tie it to something that already exists — after dinner, on the way back from an errand, a Sunday-morning circuit — so the walk happens by default rather than by negotiation.
Vary the route occasionally and keep a favourite. A familiar loop is where the ongoing conversation of a relationship quietly lives, one instalment at a time.

body.heading: Leave the phones in your pockets
paragraphs: Bring them for safety if you like, but let them stay put. A walk with two people looking at the same street is a different substance from a walk with two people looking at different feeds.
If a walk feels too quiet at first, bring one question with you — a real one, about something you genuinely wonder. Walking answers questions the way sitting rarely does.
